utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the cross-examination, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we've buried the microphone somehow. We'll get it over here. Yes, Your Honour, and I wanted to make sure that we are in private session for me to discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. Wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would first like to discuss a little bit about the mechanics of your position at the relevant period of time that we're discussing. As I understand it, you were in a platoon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to go step by step so we can -- I know you said some of these things on Friday, but just to -- this is sort of background information. And it's my understanding that that platoon was sending daily reports to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps. Is that correct? You're shaking your head. We have to make a ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I was starting out -- I was about to give my answer, and if you haven't noticed – (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I to understand that this platoon was part of or subordinated to the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This platoon was part of a company, an anti-electronic warfare company that was part of the 2nd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no brigade in between the company and the corps. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct in assuming that, yes. There was no brigade in between. We were directly subordinated to the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, at this location -- at the location where you were situated during this relevant period, and I believe it's called Okresanica -- am I pronouncing that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were other units that were listening as well, that were performing the same tasks that you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, may I just be allowed to explain -- you have just said I need to correct this. There were units that had the same purpose, had the same feature, but those units were part of other formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll going step by step, so I was just about to say: One of those units, as I understand it from your testimony on Friday, was a lower-ranking unit belonging to the 21st Division. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Precisely. I would just like to apologise, sir. When I nod, that means I am closely following your questions. That's all it means. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I figured that already. All right. Now, the 21st Division, was that part of the 2nd Corps as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st Division was directly subordinated to the 2nd Corps. The 2nd Corps was composed of a number of divisions and one of those divisions was the 21st Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was that lower-ranking unit submitting its daily reports directly to the 21st Division or were they sending them, like you, to a particular organ within the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sent their reports directly to their units, which means directly to the division. Establishment-wise, this is how it was supposed to be. I was supposed to work. I knew of this due to my knowledge of the establishment, not my knowledge of the procedures being used. Secondly, all the formations that were deployed up there had -- I need to say this again -- the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you said up there, Gore, that's up to this location where you were. That's what you mean when you say, "up there," as opposed to north, a direction of north?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the very location you're talking about, the one you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was also one unit, if we could call it that, that belonged to the services of the state security. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, they're not part of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless they were conducting the same sort of monitoring that you were, your unit was as well as the other unit that was subordinated to the 21st Division. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a unit with the same purpose, but they were part of a different formation, as I've said. I'm not sure if I should add any further explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess what I'm trying to figure out is or trying to establish I should say, you had two units that belonged to the army and you had this sort of intelligence unit, the services of the state security that belonged to the civilian government, all doing the same thing, that is monitoring conversations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were monitoring conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what I understand, sometimes all three units that were there were, in fact, monitoring the same conversation or they were -- yeah, they were monitoring the same conversation. There were instances. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said, sir. There was no way for me to know that. I had my orders, which I carried out. Back then, there was no way for me to know what their orders were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, you were aware -- let me rephrase the question. Is it not a fact that your unit would share information with the services of the state security and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last thing you said, that we exchanged information, it was a matter of agreement. As for exchanging information, I can't quite remember whether we ever obtained information from that particular service, but I know that we did give information to them because that was necessary back then. I'm not sure if there was ever any need for us to try and obtain information from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me be a little more specific. There were times, sir, that your unit would obtain monitoring information, monitoring conversations from them that you would then take and put in your daily reports and send them off to the intelligence organ of the corps. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in as far as this was the case that we did indeed obtain material from them, then it would be sent on to the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Are you saying that you never obtained material from them or are you saying when you obtained? Because I'm not here to play games. I just want a correct answer. And I understand you're an educated person, so please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've understood this correctly, I am indeed an educated person and that's why I'm trying to answer your question. They gave us information at a different location, in a different place. At the corps itself, there was a unit gathering reports. We had our own sources through which we obtained reports, and those were the reports we sent. There was no need for us at all to obtain material directly from them, because this was done in a different location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not a fact, sir, that there were times that you received monitored information, conversations, that you would then send, put in your daily report and send them to the corps expressing where that information had come from. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In as far as the head has stated that, precisely that this had been taken over from the state security service, then such material was around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't understand that answer. Sir, let me break it down. All three of you -- all three of the units were working in the same building, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm not sure why we are going back to three units now, as we are talking about two units now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But the state security unit was working right next to you in the same building, right, not in some other hill, not in some other city, but right next to you. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the same building, but they had their own entrance, the state security and their unit, the unit attached to them, as well as the unit belonging to the 21st Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were times, were there not, when you would give them information that you had gathered from your intercepting and they would do the same thing to you, they would give you information so you could pass it on to your superiors at the 2nd Corps. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, can you please try to prioritise the fact that we were the ones forwarding material to them, because they had a great interest in some of our materials that they chose themselves or selected themselves, material for them. I can't remember myself ever signing or sending the material down there. I was not the one filing the material. I was not the one analysing the material. I was a source of information, a very consistent source of information, if I may add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we go to what has been marked for identification purposes as P249. If you could first take a look at the documents, just look at them and then I will ask you some specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record I'll be looking at -- I'll be referring to P249/A, /B, /C, and /D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But please look at them. Now, sir, if you could look at the bottom of the page on the right-hand corner, you'll see the exhibit number. So when I want to make a reference to a particular page, you can look down there and that will help you out. If we could look at what has been marked for identification purposes as P249/D. And as I understand it, the English translation would be found on P249/C. That's corresponding to number 655, Your Honours. Now, with respect to this -- have you found it, sir? P249/D at the bottom. Do you see it? Is that a yes? You're shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it. I found the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go step by step. At the top, it says that it's from the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct? The very top on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it makes a reference to the corps, does it not -- not the corps, I'm sorry, the platoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And it gives us a location and also there is a date, is there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date is 16 July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, below that it says, "daily report," does it not? In the middle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you go to the next line on the left side, it says: Intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I conclude -- can we conclude that this was a daily report generated by your platoon that was being sent to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps. Can we conclude that? Just from that header, just the information I read to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm unfamiliar with this document. I don't know how the state security unit sent documents to our unit, but this looks very much like one of those, if that pleases you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting, sir, that at the top portion that we just covered, that that's coming from the state security? Is that what you are suggesting? Is this not, sir, a daily report sent by your platoon to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You're not certain. All right. If we go -- as you see there's some dotted lines all the way across the page, and then below it we see some letters and a date, and the date is 17 July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the letters that are above it reflect -- those are the initials of the security services, are they not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to this line of questioning. The witness just indicated that he doesn't really seem to recollect the document. I'm not entirely sure if he's now in a position to answer questions to are specific to the document if he doesn't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this document was used in the direct examination. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, Your Honour. I didn't actually put it to the witness. I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was not put to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- but anyway, we'll see whether the witness could answer this question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials, yes or no, the ones that I just showed to you that are on the left side of the page immediately below the dotted line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These initials refer to the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same service that we were discussing earlier. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so -- now if we could look at what has been marked for identification purposes as P249/B, if we could look at that. Now, at the top of the page we have those same initials that we saw on the previous document, which was 249/D. Do you see that? CSB/SDB Tuzla, the date 17 July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first line immediately below what would appear to be the number 652 that was given to these sets of conversations, they indicate the frequency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the first message is numbered 652, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- well, just for the record, could you please read the first line under 652. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, if you want to use this piece of document, my advice is to have it translated into English. Because here we only have the 655.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And here's my point, if I may. The Prosecution has contended and they presented their documents suggesting that 655 was actually a conversation that took place on the 16th. Based on the document that I just presented to this gentleman, which would be 249/D1. What is clear is that this conversation was actually recorded by the security services on the 17th. They then received that information from the security services, and in their daily report, they put down July 16, as opposed to 17. That's the point that I wish to make with respect to this and also to show that the gentleman was incorrect or perhaps his memory is somewhat faded when he indicated that he had not received information or they were not sharing information from the security services with respect to messages that they had been intercepting. And I'm going to show other intercepts to show that it was a two-way cooperation with respect to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But at this place we have a language problem, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I'll just ask the following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that 655 comes after 652?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow, sir, these conversations were not familiar to me. It was precisely these that I was not acquainted with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, a specific question was posed to you. Does 655 come after --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. First of all, in Mr. Karnavas's submissions to you he indicated that the witness said that the information wasn't given to him or something to that effect. First of all, I think the witness had said in his evidence that he didn't recall whether he had received such information. So that's a mischaracterisation. Secondly, I think the witness is now attempting to explain something, which he's entitled to do, rather than being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I posed a question. The witness is entitled to answer the question and if he wishes to explain, he can explain. The question was: Does 655 come after 652? That's all the -- that was the question and it doesn't call for an explanation, Your Honour. But I can move on if the Court wishes for me to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, can you answer that question? It's a specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand the question correctly, does material number 655 come directly after 652, I see a number of things in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't insert the word "directly," but in any event, I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned you never saw that document that was provided to us from the Prosecution. Is that correct though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me, I'll never tire of saying this. I'll be just as persistent as you are. I do not remember this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you have never seen it? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: How is he going to answer that question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you have to give a direct answer. It's very -- just a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can you just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing the document, sir, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can I conclude that the Prosecution in prepping you to come and testify did not show this document to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The top part of that document where it talked about daily reports, did that look familiar to you? Not the contents, but just the top portion of the document. Would that be consistent with the language that you -- or the information that you would put down in daily reports when you sent them to the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to point one thing out, though, are you talking about conversation number 652 or 655 or are you talking about the document as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's not the same form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I have to warn you, look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated on direct examination the procedure, and I want to go through the procedure a little bit. As I understand it, you're not an analyst. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you got that right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not there to analyse the information, but merely to make sure that you could pick up conversations, in other words, monitor the frequencies, pick them up, record them, and send them off. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As faithfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the basic procedure was that as soon as you could locate a conversation, you would immediately begin to record it -- not you personally, but your staff, everybody in that platoon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "usual"? Was there another practice too that we haven't talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the regular practice. There were also extraordinary cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "extraordinary cases," you mean that they weren't recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You misunderstood me. What happened was that several conversations would be recorded at once. The first one would be at zero position on the recording device, and then apart from the regular data such as the channel frequency, participants, and so on, the data that would be entered would be from what point to what point on the counter. The conversation was recorded. So they would be recorded in sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is that the first step in this process is the recording of a conversation, you first record it. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by that you mean that at the moment a conversation was registered, yes, the recording would begin at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And by that I mean the tape recording. Then the next step would be to listen to the tape recording and to try to write down as faithfully as you could what was on the tape, what had been picked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sometimes the conversations were rather clear and so you could write them directly into the notebooks as you were hearing the tape recording, as the tape was being played, that is. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were conversations of this sort, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there were other conversations where you could not quite make out what was being said, and so, as you indicated, like a deejay, you would have to play it over and over again until you would try to figure out exactly what was being said. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those would be recorded -- those would be transcribed initially on pieces of paper until you were comfortable that it was a true, accurate, and complete transcription of the conversation before you would write them into the notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's what I understood you to have said on Friday. So please tell me, what was the actual procedure in instances where the recording was poor -- of a poor quality and you were trying to figure out the exact words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain it several times, if need be. When we received a conversation that was very difficult to transcribe, we would say it was very difficult to take down, we would listen to that material sentence by sentence, word by word, stop and go back, and then we would put it down in the notebook. There was no reason to write it down on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I misunderstood. And there were times, I take it, that you had some difficulty in quite understanding what was being said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next step -- incidentally, when you are writing it out, on the choice of punctuation, whether you put a comma, a period, an exclamation point, was there any set procedure or was it left up to the discretion of the person who was trying to interpret or transcribe what was from the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were required with regard to details such as when someone raised their voice, we would have to put an exclamation mark there. If there was a question, we would use a question mark. When there was a pause, we would use a comma. Several points, several dots, would mean that we had been unable to understand a part and to transcribe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was everyone educated equally, that is, those who were performing those tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). And I don't need the specific ones of each one, but what was the range of education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part it was secondary school. That was the mean level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, the next step was once you had transcribed what had been on the tape, the next step would be to give it to somebody else and that they would type it out. It would go to the KZU operator to be encrypted so then it could be sent out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the procedure you have just described was the one what was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, those who were operating the KZU were not the same folks, such as yourself, that were monitoring, recording, and transcribing the conversations that you had been able to pick up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have to be radio operators in order to monitor conversations. You are quite right, there was more than one person there. And some of the operators even worked on KZU.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I mentioned this because you've indicated on direct examination that the transcription from the tape conversations into the notebooks were verbatim. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then when they went from the notebook to be then typed out, you had nothing to do with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the typed version -- when the messages were actually typed out, was there any quality control in a sense that they would come back to you or to your colleagues to check to make sure that what was typed out matched what had been written out into the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they came back. So you would read it, make sure that it was true, accurate, and complete before it went out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document would be on the computer screen from where the operator who had received the document would look at it and compare it with the transcript in the notebook. He would then say "Yes, this is correct." There were more problems that had to do with the KZU operator being unable to read a word, then he would ask -- he would go back to the person who had written it to explain it to him or to read the text to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was slightly different, in other words, somebody other than the typist would not then look at it to make sure that it was absolutely accurate before it was sent out? In other words, a clean set of eyes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another check that followed in the command. This check would be carried out after the documents and the notebooks that had been archived were compared, as were the tapes we had handed in. So the entire material would be reviewed again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the answer to my question, though, is no? At the platoon where you were before something went out, there was nobody that independently checked after it was typed out to make sure that the typed version matched what was in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- yes, I see you're insisting on this question, and the correct reply is that I carried out spot checks of the material, but I was not able to check everything. I wasn't there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And I take it, if we could go further back into the process, after somebody had transcribed what was on the tape, there was no, shall we put it, clean set of ears to do another quality check to ensure that what was on the tape actually was put down on the paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it today, as we stand here, we do not have any tapes that we could listen to that would give us some comfort, assurances, that what was actually put down matches verbatim to what was heard and transcribed and typed out and sent and brought here in court today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this question is put to Prosecution but not to witness. How could the witness answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he could answer if he knows that the tapes exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may try that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the tapes after they got filled? Did you preserve them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. That was not your previous question. If you're asking me that now, I will be pleased to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- I'll break it down. Were the tapes preserved so we have some archive of all the tapes, of all the intercepts that filled those 30 notebooks that we have here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot know this. Let me answer your previous question as to where the tapes were sent. When the tapes were filled, they were sent to the commander of my unit; that's where they went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So they were not re-used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received tapes that had been previously used. I'm speaking of some of the tapes. So some tapes were new, others were being re-used. For example, the radio station which had lots of tapes and were able to give us some, they used a different speed so that it was not a problem to record over and there were no problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But when you record over or you erase and record over, it's fair to say that what was originally recorded is lost. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't know what kind of tapes you use, but the ones that I'm familiar with are the ones that you could puncture at the top on the one side to make sure that they cannot be re-recorded, in other words, what's on it stays, so by accident you can't erase any portion of it. Was that procedure used by your platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the tapes or the cassettes, just to clarify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- well, maybe you can help me out here. When you were tape recording, were you using a reel-to-reel or were you using these little cassettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reel-to-reel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And not the little cassettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then you would send off those reels along with the notebooks at some point to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not necessarily sent together as a single package, but yes, they were sent to the command. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just one last question on this area. Were there occasions where you would -- where there might be a shortage and you on your own would go ahead and erase the reel in order to re-record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to try and remember. I know there was a shortage of reels and I also know that there was a period of time when we did have this situation. This was when there was very little activity and we would even erase our own reels. But those that had already been sent to the command, those were the ones we would erase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since then have you had the opportunity to see those reels that you had sent off to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it as far as you are concerned, you don't know what happened to those or where they are, if they still exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tapes were sent to the command. What happened to them further was not my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never suggested they were. And I take it, in working with the Office of the Prosecution they have never shown you any reels for you to listen to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I have to ask. All right. All right. Now, if I could -- if we could go to what has been marked as P231 for identification purposes. I believe this was a document shown to you on Friday. And we're just going to cover some technical matters. First I'd just like you to look at all of these pages that are attached as part of 231, and you should have them labelled as A, B, C, D, and E. Just take a look at them, and then for the record I'm going to try to explain what they are before we jump into them. Okay. Now, if we look at 231/B at the bottom on the right-hand corner you'll see a B. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be the original transcription from the notebook. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we look to A, what has been marked as A, it's in English. And I understand from Friday where you corrected the screen at one point, you must read English, could you look at it to see whether, in fact, this is a translation of B.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I don't think we can presume that the witness actually reads English. What he corrected was a numerical point or a number from the screen. I don't think that's a fair question. Having said that, it's obviously a translation. I don't think that is going to be in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that was the dispute. When his direct testimony was going on. It was about the dialect between the KZU and the original transcribed conversation. It was a dialect matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let us see what is the question. What is the point that Mr. Karnavas is going to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Do you know whether -- can you read English? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't understand or -- the question is: Do you read English? Not whether you understand English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With great difficulty, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Then I want to ask you the next series of questions. Then let's look at what has been marked as P231/D. Now, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it not the same -- is it not a translation or a typed version of what was -- what is in 231/B? I'll tell you what, why don't I withdraw that question and I'll ask you another question. Okay. Do you see -- if I could point your direction -- if I could point your attention to what has been marked as 231/E. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document is a daily report, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this daily report is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if we can remove that document from the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document is a transcription of what is in 231/B, is it not? If you can just take a good look at it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but which is a transcription of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well -- all right. B is the handwritten version, correct? B, the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a copy of the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: E, the one that says E has the same text that is in the handwritten version, but it's typed and it's in a daily report generated by your platoon and sent to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now before we get to this document and discuss it, all right, before we get to it, I want you to look at what has been marked as D, 231/D. And for right now, I would like you to just focus on the language, the text itself. Is the text of the message not the same -- is it not the same as the text that's in 231/E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is that document 231/E is typed in both capital and small letters, while D is typed out only in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But the message itself, what was -- what is being sent is the same. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus our attention just a tiny but on D. If you look at the left-hand corner, at the top of the page, we see a number, right, 626, do we not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have the date. Correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did this document come from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the line of text just underneath the date, we can see that this is from a state security report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we conclude that they either listened to the same conversation or your platoon passed this information on to the state security services?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says very clearly, taken over from PEB of the 2nd Corps, which means that this is our material that we sent on to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely, which is exactly the question I had asked you earlier, was there not occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not the question that he asked earlier. I think now Mr. Karnavas is misstating the evidence. What he asked him was whether the army took information from the state security, not vice versa. He's already testified about this in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think if we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's not go back to the previous statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You just ask your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So here is one piece of document demonstrating, does it not, that material was given by your platoon to the security services that were in the same building but in another room so that they could pass it on to their handlers, their superiors, while you were sending yours to the intelligence organ. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, incidentally I should point out for the record that C is a translation of D and C, at the top of the page, it does say, "Adopted from 2nd Corps," which is what the gentleman had just read from D. Now, am I to understand correctly, Your Honours, that about this time we take a break or do I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- feel it convenient, we'll break now. Which means, did you finish this part of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've finished this part but not this entire intercept. But I finished this part. This would be an excellent point to stop unless you want to give me another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we'll break now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just wonder if we can go into private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe when we left off, we were discussing what was marked for identification purposes as P231. And if you could be so kind as to -- I'm going to be referring to B and E, and in the English version it would be A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Your Honour, that A is a direct translation of B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, just again as I understand it, those who were typing out the handwritten messages, they were not at liberty to make corrections and had to type out exactly what was written out in the notebooks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go through this document and point out a few matters and perhaps you can assist us here. If I'm correct, you've been handed a copy that has some markings on it or highlighted. Is that correct? Are there any highlights to those documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at the handwritten version to, one, two, three, four, five, I believe it's the fifth or the sixth line, there's one particular word, and in the English version it would be one, two, three, four, five, six. And I'm particularly focusing on the sentence that says: "How can I find out where General Zivanovic is?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, and I'm not an expert in your language, but as I understand it, that is of the dialect that is commonly known as Ekavski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at what was trans -- what was typed out in the daily report, as I understand it, it's in the other dialect, the Ijekavski is that correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So here we can say that there is a discrepancy, can we not? Minor as it may be, nonetheless there is a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you in that respect, sir, but there is a grammatical discrepancy, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I didn't pick that one out. Do you want to share that with us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what you just said, the words "gde" and "gdje," both mean the same thing, but in two different dialects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we went further down in the handwritten version, and it's further down in the English in the sentence where it says: "Yes, yes. I understand you." Do you see that? It's further down towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again we see the same error, do we not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But then the same words are used correctly, as I understand it, further down, where it says "Razumem." It would be on the next page, the first line. Is that correct? There they corrected themselves. They're using the correct dialect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then again I just -- it's a minor point, but I just wanted to point it out that in the sentence on the second page in English where it says: "I understand. I'm going to the post up there." In the handwritten version where it says "gore," "up there," the last word, there is no period, probably an oversight, whereas when it was transcribed, there is a period there. Do you see that? It's on the second page, sir. Where it says: "I understand. I'm going to my post up there." In the handwritten version, there's no period; whereas, in the typed version there is a period. Is that correct? On the second page --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I couldn't find it immediately, but I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now -- so there's no period in the handwritten version. Correct? I mean, it's an oversight, no drama.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the copy that I have, there is no period. I'm not sure about the original, but this document that I have in front of me now does not have a period there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But if you look at the type-written version, you will find a period, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could just focus our attention slightly on that particular sentence, and I'm going to read it in English and you follow along. It says: "I understand. I'm going to my post up there." In the handwritten version you see the period after the word "I understand," is that correct? We're still on the same sentence, sir, on the second page. If you could look at the handwritten version. Right after the words "I understand," there is a period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we also not put a comma there? "I understand, I'm going to my post up there." Would that also not work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could easily tell if you had a chance to listen to the recorded conversation. If you look at the transcript, it's a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, we don't have that, see, that's the problem. Okay. So in other words, as you sit here today you cannot tell us whether a comma could easily fit into where that period is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we're going to go to another set of documents if that's okay. And I would like to direct your attention to the other document that was presented to you on Friday, and that's P232 that was marked for identification purposes. And if you could just look at them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, just to save a little bit of time, and the Prosecutor can correct me if I'm wrong, but it's my understanding that what has been marked as 232/A is a translation of what has been marked as 232/C is a translation of /D. And /D is a typed version of /B. And /E is a daily report with the contents of /D. I'll try to lay a foundation to the witness, but I think I have it right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, if you could look at what has been marked as /B first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me that /B is the handwritten version. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were to look at /E, at the top of the page again it shows that this is a daily report having been generated from your platoon being forwarded to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we go into the content, if you could look at /D, what has been marked as 232/D, and I believe the English translation is /C. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who generated this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the form of this document, it is obvious that it was not generated by my unit. The material being referred to is the same material that we had in front of us just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So another unit came up with this -- made this document? Or was this shared by your unit to another unit? If you can help us out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way for me to know that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. So we won't discuss them. Now, let's look at, as I promised, /A, /B, and /E. Okay. And I would like you to focus on /B and /E while the rest of us also look at /A, which is the English translation. The first line says: "Hello, Badem. Let me talk to Beara." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I don't have the comma after hello.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you're absolutely right. That's in the English version. Somebody put it there, whoever transcribed it. In the handwritten version there is no comma after hello, right, but there is a period after Badem. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we not also put a comma there, "Hello Badem, let me talk to Beara."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I never gave this any thought whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But grammatically speaking, and I'm not suggesting that you should have given it any thought, but grammatically speaking --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I understand my friend has asked a number of questions in this line and I haven't objected to this point, but I just don't see the relevance of this and I just don't know how much longer we're going to be dealing with this particular issue of grammar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's unfortunate the Prosecutor doesn't sit here every day when we take evidence, but there was last week, for instance, one particular intercept where the witness did indicate that it all depends on where you put the comma, and whether it has a comma there or period. So that's the whole purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. What's the point in that particular content?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to suggest, Your Honour -- rather, what I'm trying to prove is that the person who is writing it down is making a -- it's at his discretion whether he puts a period or a comma after certain words or phrases. And so, because of the testimony of the other witness last week, he gave one interpretation depending on whether you have a period. He said it has another interpretation if you have a comma. I'm trying to suggest that we have no way of verifying of whether a comma or a period should be up there -- should be on the paper. It fits well within the theory of my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if the document puts a full stop there, then it's a full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but at the same time if the witnesses is willing to say that he gave it not thought and that grammatically a comma could go as well as a full stop, obviously, that -- it all depends -- the interpretation of the document depends on who put it there and what are the reasons. If it's just pure by accident, then the Prosecution should not be able to say, "Well, there's a full stop there, therefore, this particular meaning should apply."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you going -- we are at the very beginning of this document. Are you going to each sentence and paragraph and challenge that full stop? There must be a point, you know. You may raise in a particular sentence in a theme and ask a question to this witness, whether there should be a comma or full stop. If you have a case, you know. You cannot go like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to be disrespectful and I certainly don't want to argue the point, but if a Prosecutor is going to stand up here and say: "This is the interpretation for this particular intercept because the witness said this is how I interpreted it because there is a period there." And have another witness who is taking the intercepts and saying "Well, yes, a comma could go here or a period could go here." And if I don't have the tapes, as the gentleman indicated, it all depends from listening to the tapes, then I think there is a dilemma as far as the Tribunal is concerned, the Trial Chamber is concerned as to whether to accept one interpretation versus the other. And where there is doubt, that has to go in favour of the Defence, not in favour of the Prosecution. That is my point. And I need to make a record so that at the closing argument in my submission brief I can show there were instances where based on the individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, don't wait until that time. You have a particular case in this conversation, in these intercepts. Just a point to that particular place and ask a question to this witness. But don't go paragraph -- sentence by sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are only two or three sentences, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Believe me, I can go through all the intercepts and point out thousands of discrepancies. These are just little vignettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed with the witness. We'll see how far it can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go further down, there's one indication where it says "Duty officer." Do you see that? Further down, a few lines further down in the handwritten version there is no comma but in the typed version, the person typing it inserted a comma. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me check this, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to referring to the sentence, the duty officer of Palma needs him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where it says: "Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the duty officer." That's the one. "I'm the duty officer at Palma." At Palma.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the Palma duty officer." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on to another one. Further down in the page you say: "Hello. Hello." There's one section. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Hello, hello."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you have periods there. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Are you referring to the part of the text where it says: "I will, I will. Hello. Hello." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you have a hello. Then there is a period. Then the next hello is on the next line. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have periods there; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the written text. You mean after every word there's a period. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the document. Look at the one that is handwritten. It says: "Hello. Hello." Am I correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've just explained it very well. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at the type-written version in your daily report.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says: "Hello! Hello!"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is different, is it not, the type-written version from the handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are going to go into these tiny little details, then there are some extremely minor differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you have to explain to us what is the difference by changing those exclamation marks and full stop. I just fail to see that unless you pointed to a particular place where the meaning of the sentence will be totally changed if we changed those full stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be more than happy to argue this point outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean it's a legal question, not a specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting, Your Honour, is by providing an answer to your question the witness may be influenced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have some technical problems because the transcript. Would you please stop here. Well, Mr. Karnavas, you haven't finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I don't want to do is telegraph where I'm going to this witness. And I think it's important that I be able to argue my point of relevance to the Court without giving the witness an opportunity to see where I'm going with my line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the instruction from the Chamber is you point to that particular place where if somebody changed that comma into full stop, the meaning will be totally different. I just want you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that there is a lot of grammar discrepancies. There is no problem about it. But the problem is that you have to direct our attention to that particular place, which might be relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm trying to suggest, and maybe, I'm being inarticulate today, is that the person who is writing these things down is using his or her discretion as to whether to put a full stop or a comma. I understand you're asking me to show that there would be a different meaning. That's not the purpose of this cross-examination. The purpose is to show that they make a discretion. And on one particular intercept that's critical to us, the Prosecution has a witness who says it all depends on whether you put a period or a comma. What I'm trying to suggest is and I even indicated this in my cross-examination, that where that comma was a period could be inserted, or vice versa. I don't recall the instance. In other words, it all depends on where the person who is taking the information decides to put it, because they're getting this information. They're not analysing it. That's not the purpose of it. So that's all I'm trying to demonstrate here so I can have a foundation so later on I can make my argue as to reasonable doubt with respect to one particular piece of evidence. And I certainly don't mean to take up the Court's time. Also, there was an instance where this witness indicated that everything is taken down verbatim. What we can see is that discrepancies do exist. In one particular instance, in the next document I'm going to show, they even insert an expletive that wasn't recorded. I don't know if this satisfies the Court, but I certainly don't mean to be argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's come to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to what has been marked for identification purposes as P245. And for the record, if I may, and I can be can corrected if I'm wrong 245/A is a translation of /B, /D is the typed version of /B and /C is the translation of /D. Sir, if you can look at these documents first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking at these documents. And let me add, I did not draft these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. But you're here, are you not, as the -- we may need to go into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the intercepts that were monitored and recorded by the security services had a number, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas the intercepts that you recorded in the notebooks did not have a number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. What numbers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number to the particular intercept, like intercept number 655. When you would -- you had your notebooks and as the intercepts were coming in, you were recording them. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to have missed the fact that this is a document not generated in my unit. It may have come through a different channel. Number 646 and so on, these were numbers entered by a different unit and there are other people you can ask about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear my question, though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were talking about numbers above the text, number 642 or 645.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go simple on you. In your notebooks, any notebook, before an intercept was written out, did you put a number on it or did you just write in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we noted the frequency, the time, the participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the answer to my question is: No, you did not give it a number. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't give it a number. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Whereas the security services would give numbers as we saw, such as 655, the one that I showed you earlier. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'm showing you right now, does it have a number that would give us the indication --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- I'm entitled to ask my question and then if she hears the question, then she can object. Otherwise, I will indulge in the same form of objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You may finish your questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in looking at this document, we don't see a number, and from that can we not conclude that most likely it is not from the security services?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm objecting because counsel has now framed his question a very misleading manner. We have already established that there were other platoons that were monitoring and intercepting communications other than the state security services and other than the one we're dealing with currently. So I think it's very misleading to put the form of the question in that manner without indicating that there are other platoons who were doing the same work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously the Prosecutor has not listened to the question, because it's a process of elimination. First, I want to eliminate the security services --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then I go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand. But your question makes it very difficult to understand because you used two negative terms and when translated into another language it will be a disaster. So you use the simplest language to ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And if I could, Your Honour, with the Court's indulgence, if I could consult my co-counsel with respect to a matter concerning what we're talking about right now. Ten seconds

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have before me what has been marked as Exhibit P327, and perhaps if I -- if the gentleman could be shown my particular copy, if he -- if you could just look at the front -- the first page, perhaps this may clarify this. And I'm not -- would you just look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you have to tell us what are the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a document given to us by the Prosecution, and it is the cover of a notebook. And then there is a sequencing of the pages that are numbered. And it would appear that the document that I am referring to was part of that notebook. So if indeed this notebook was one of theirs, then it would stand to reason that the document that I'm showing the gentleman is a document that was generated by his unit. So I don't know if he's able to clarify that matter. If he can, fine. If he cannot, then I won't push the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having looked at the front page, does that appear to be a cover of a notebook generated by your unit? If you could look at that and maybe the following few pages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do not recognise the front page of this notebook. Just let me mention in passing that we did have another location where the same work was conducted that we did. So within the company, there were two such platoons. There was an identical platoon to ours working in a different location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did they use the same sort of notebooks as you did? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. That's your conclusion, sir. You said the same kind of notebook. Are you referring to the way entries were made or are you referring to the same type of paper, the same type of binding, the same physical notebook? Would you be clearer, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, had I asked you the question: Were they filling out the notebooks in the same manner, then you would understand exactly what I was asking. My question was: Did they use the same types of notebooks that you used? And from that one can only conclude that what I'm asking is physically, were they physically the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really not necessary to be sarcastic in asking questions. I think, you know, the witness is trying to clarify something he didn't understand. It was a legitimate question and it's totally unnecessary to behave in this manner. And I don't think it's respectful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness is being less than responsive and is playing with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I told you that you should ask a very simple question. And if there's a problem of translation and you have to understand that. I believe both of us are not experts in that language at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the document that you have before you, does it appear to be the same kind of notebook, copy of a notebook, that you were using?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see that this is not a document I had, not a notebook I had. It's not a notebook I filled in. I really don't want to answer this question because there are other people from the unit who could give you a reply to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the size of the document that I've shown you the same size as the notebooks that you were using? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
